title: Business Management HL · Set B · Paper 3
subject: business-management

resources.title: Resource 1 · The mission of NightBridge
resources.text: NightBridge is a social enterprise providing safe late-evening transport for shift workers in a rural district. Its constitution requires at least 60% of passenger journeys to be offered to eligible low-income workers at a maximum fare of CU 2. Last year it carried 30,000 passenger journeys. Eighteen thousand six hundred were concession journeys. Six paid drivers work with volunteers who coordinate stops. A driver says that helping workers keep jobs motivates her to stay, but unpredictable schedules are exhausting.

resources.title: Resource 2 · Cash and capacity
resources.text: NightBridge has unrestricted cash of CU 42,000. At its current activity it expects an operating cash deficit of CU 3,000 a month before the options below. Its board requires a minimum unrestricted balance of CU 12,000. Two minibuses are heavily used between 21:00 and 23:00. A spare vehicle can run only if another qualified driver is available. Another district operator would lease a bus for CU 3,000 per month, excluding driver wages.

resources.title: Resource 3 · Employer proposal
resources.text: A manufacturer offers a 12-month paid service for its employees. It would add 6,000 full-fare passenger journeys per year and CU 5,500 monthly net cash inflow from month 2 after ordinary operating costs, including a driver. Driver training and route preparation would cost CU 15,000 immediately. The manufacturer wants regular departures during the current peak. It will consider moving half its departures 30 minutes later. Under its initial timetable, existing concession journeys fall by 1,200 annually and the remaining existing journeys are unchanged. The contract is renewable but the employer gives no commitment beyond year one.

resources.title: Resource 4 · Passenger survey and council offer
resources.text: In a survey of 90 current concession passengers, 54 work rotating shifts and 63 say a fixed late departure would make travel less useful. The volunteers reached passengers on two busy nights. A council offers a restricted CU 24,000 training grant for relief drivers over one year. Training costs exactly CU 24,000 and does not cover wages, buses or existing deficits. A six-week pilot of staggered employer departures could run with a smaller contract; its net receipts would need to be negotiated. The council wants verified monthly concession proportions, missed pick-ups and staff turnover before discussing renewal.

questions.title: NightBridge · Social enterprise
questions.stem: Use all four resources in planning your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using one motivation theory, describe a human need that NightBridge helps a driver meet.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two challenges NightBridge faces in maintaining social and financial sustainability.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Recommend a two-year plan of action that improves NightBridge’s finances while meeting its social purpose. Refer to all the resources and use relevant business management tools or theory.

steps.text: Identify a relevant need and theory, such as relatedness under Alderfer or belonging under Maslow.
The driver’s role connects her to workers who depend on the service. Accept esteem or another need if convincingly linked to the evidence.
The unrestricted cash buffer is CU 30,000.
At CU 3,000 per month it reaches the floor after ten months without improvement.
The council grant is restricted to training and cannot cover the recurring deficit.
The employer adds full-fare journeys and displaces eligible passengers during peak hours.
The initial timetable gives 17,400 concession journeys out of 34,800, or 50%, below 60%.
Accepting without redesign could breach the constitution precisely when shift workers need access. Credit other distinct applied challenges, up to three marks each.

Resource use (0–4). At 1 refer to a resource, at 2 apply some case evidence, at 3 connect most of it to the plan, at 4 integrate all four resources. Link peak capacity, driver motivation, the cash floor, the employer’s offer, the survey and the restricted grant to decisions.

Tools and theory (0–4). Move from naming a tool (1) to partial application (2), sound application (3) and effective decision use (4). Paying CU 15,000 leaves CU 27,000 before month-one operations, then CU 24,000 at the end of that month. From month 2 the full offer produces a net CU 2,500 monthly surplus. It violates the concession condition as offered. At existing full-fare volumes of 17,400 after expansion, meeting 60% would require 26,100 concession journeys, 8,700 above the initial forecast. Adjust either side of that ratio and re-cost the revised timetable.

Evaluation (0–6). Award 1–2 for an asserted option, 3–4 for comparing plausible effects, and 5–6 for a case-specific judgement that weighs feasibility, stakeholder effects and uncertainties. Negotiate off-peak timing, a cap on full-fare capacity or employer support for additional concession seats. Extra training alone cannot fund wages. The pilot and two-night survey give incomplete evidence, so consult workers on other shifts and monitor missed pickups. Holding the full contract until revised cash and journey targets are credible is defensible.

Action and sequence (0–3). Award 1 for isolated actions, 2 for a workable sequence, 3 for linked milestones and contingencies. Before signing, agree financing, timings and protected concessions. Monitor cash, service access and driver retention monthly during the pilot. Scale only once forecasts clear the CU 12,000 floor and the 60% test. During year two diversify employers and seek replacement training support if the council or manufacturer withdraws. Accept other supported sequences and conclusions.
